minimumBid.title: Lowest bid allowed
minimumBid.help: The smallest contract the auction will accept. Seven is a majority of the thirteen tricks; lowering it makes contracts easier to win and harder to make.

bidTime.title: Bidding Time
bidTime.help: How long each player gets to bid. If the clock runs out, they pass.

rules.title: Rules
description: Tarneeb is played by four people in two teams of two, with partners sitting opposite each other. Every card of a standard 52-card deck is dealt, so everybody holds thirteen.
Before a card is played the table **bids**: each player in turn says how many of the thirteen tricks their team will take, or passes. Once you pass you are out of the bidding for that round.

bidding.title: Bidding
description: Every bid has to beat the one before it, and the lowest bid allowed is seven — a majority of the tricks. Being outbid does not put you out: you get another turn, and you can take the contract back.
The last player still in wins the auction, names the **trump** suit and leads the first trick. If all four pass, the hand is thrown in and dealt again.

trump.title: Trump and following suit
description: Everybody has to **follow suit** if they can; only a player holding none of the suit that was led may play something else. You are never forced to trump.
The highest trump played takes the trick. If nobody trumped it, the highest card of the suit that was led wins. Aces are high.

scoring.title: Scoring
description: If the bidding team takes at least as many tricks as it bid, it scores a point for every trick it took and the other team scores nothing. If it falls short, it **loses** the amount it bid and the other team scores a point for each of their own tricks.
Taking all thirteen on a smaller bid is a **Kaboot** and pays three extra. Bidding all thirteen and making it is worth 26; failing it costs 16 and pays the opponents double.

bots.title: Bots
description: Easy bots talk themselves into contracts they cannot make, and play any card the rules allow. Normal bots bid what their hand is worth and read the trick in front of them: they stay out of a partner's winning trick and take the rest as cheaply as they can.

Hard bots count the cards. They remember which suits you have run out of, which high cards are gone, and which suits you have chosen to lead — so leading a suit at your partner twice is something they will answer.
